title: The Punjab years
hook: violence by militants and by police killed people across Punjab; a human-rights worker, Jaswant Singh Khalra, documented disappearances and was killed

segments.voice: Yesterday, widows' colony, and your line was they raised them alone. Did you do one practical thing for someone raising a child? Today the story goes back to Punjab, into the hardest years. Day one thousand fourteen.

A ledger in a city office: dates, firewood, and a line that says unidentified. Then another line, and another. The cremation ground keeps records of the wood it buys to burn the dead. A man from Amritsar named Jaswant Singh Khalra asked to see those records. He began adding up the lines marked unidentified, and he began asking a simple, dangerous question: who were they? Today, the years when Punjab burned from more than one side, and the man who counted the missing.
screen: `A LEDGER: FIREWOOD, UNIDENTIFIED.` → `WHO WERE THEY?` → `THE MAN WHO COUNTED.`

segments.voice: First, the violence from one side. After the June and the November, armed militants fighting for a separate Sikh state called Khalistan killed police and officials, and they also killed ordinary people: Hindus, and Sikhs who disagreed with them. Buses were stopped. Markets were bombed. Second, the violence from the other. Police fighting the militants were given wide powers, and young Sikh men were picked up, tortured, killed in staged encounters, or simply disappeared. Families went to police stations and were told their sons had never been there. Both of these are part of the record, and Punjab's families carry both. Third, the counting. Jaswant Singh Khalra worked for the human rights wing of the Akali Dal. He went through cremation ground records in Amritsar district and found bodies cremated as unidentified, lines he believed were the disappeared. He published what he found and spoke about it, in India and abroad. Then he himself was taken from outside his home and killed. Police officers were later convicted for his abduction and murder. That's today's line: he counted the missing. Fourth, the root. In the hymns Guru Nanak sang about the violence of Babur's armies, at Ang 723, he says that he speaks the word of truth, and will tell the truth at the time for truth. Khalra did not pick up a weapon. He picked up a ledger. He is remembered for that.
screen: `MILITANTS KILLED POLICE AND CIVILIANS.` · `POLICE TORTURE AND DISAPPEARANCES.` · `KHALRA OPENED THE LEDGERS.` · `ANG 723: TRUTH AT THE TIME FOR TRUTH.` · then, large: `HE COUNTED THE MISSING.`

segments.voice: Two minutes to honor someone who told the truth. Sit still for a moment, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who told a hard truth when it cost them: a whistleblower, a journalist, a friend who said what no one else would, maybe someone in your own family. Breathe in, and see their face. Breathe out, and thank them, silently. Then ask yourself what one small truth you have been keeping quiet. You don't have to act on it now. Just hold it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Khalra. The Amritsar man who read cremation ledgers, counted the disappeared of the Punjab years, and was killed for it. Today's word.
Your line: he counted the missing. Today, read or share the true story of one person who was disappeared or silenced somewhere, so their name is counted once more. Day one thousand fourteen.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Jaswant Singh Khalra as a defender of human rights; families of the disappeared and human rights groups continue to seek records and justice for those killed in these years.
